title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 375
paragraphs: While this Psammis was king of Egypt, envoys came to him from the Eleians, who boasted that they arranged the Olympic contest in the most just and honorable manner possible, and thought that not even the Egyptians, the wisest of men, could devise anything else to be added to their rules. When the Eleians came to Egypt and stated what they had come for, the king called together those of the Egyptians reputed to be the wisest, and when the Egyptians had gathered, they heard the Eleians describe everything it was their duty to do concerning the contest. After they had explained everything, they said they had come to learn what else the Egyptians might find to suggest, anything juster than this. The Egyptians, after consulting together, asked the Eleians whether their own citizens took part in the contest, and they answered that it was permitted to anyone who wished, both of their own people and of the other Greeks equally, to compete. Upon this the Egyptians said that in arranging the games this way they had utterly missed the mark of justice; for it could not be otherwise than that they would side with the man of their own state if he were competing, and thus act unfairly to the stranger. If they really wished, as they claimed, to arrange the games justly, and if this was the reason they had come to Egypt, they advised them to arrange the contest so that only foreigners might compete in it, and no Eleian would be allowed to compete. Such was the suggestion made by the Egyptians to the Eleians.
